content.p: On the morning of 27 December 1994, just after Christmas, the commercial heart of Mokokchung, a hill town in Nagaland, was set on fire. Local accounts say soldiers of the 16th Maratha Light Infantry, joined by a section of the 10th Assam Rifles, killed civilians, burned shops with people inside them, assaulted townspeople and destroyed dozens of buildings after a lieutenant colonel of their battalion was shot dead near the Main Police Point. People in the town call the day Ayatai, an Ao expression for extreme grief and mourning that, in the words of the Morung Express, has no exact English equivalent.

Almost everything about the day is disputed, from the number of dead to who fired first. The army's side survives in thin form, in a tribute to the dead officer written by a retired brigadier. The townspeople's side was set down in an open letter, a student statement from Delhi, a complaint to the National Human Rights Commission and three decades of anniversary testimony. The Morung Express describes the event as one of many military excesses in the Naga hills that were never acknowledged in Delhi, and its survivors say no one has been tried for it.
content.h2: A town in the Naga conflict
content.p: Mokokchung had lived beside the Indo-Naga political conflict for decades. Speaking at the 2024 vigil, Lanukaba Imchen, who owned a shop in the town in 1994, recalled that by 1956 almost all Ao villages except a few had been burned in the struggle, and he pointed to the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act of 1958, which in his words gave the army sweeping powers and impunity. The Act allows an officer of any rank, in an area declared disturbed, to fire even to the point of causing death in specified circumstances. A writer in the Morung Express argued that this is why soldiers of junior rank felt free to open fire in the town.

In late December 1994 the town was in a holiday mood. A Morung Express writer who retold a survivor's recollection noted that the town square had hosted the annual Christmas cake race barely a week earlier. Another writer described a young government servant out shopping that morning, in the wedding and holiday season, when people were about in the town centre.

Imchen told the 2024 gathering that telephone lines had been cut early in the morning and that soldiers entered houses under the pretext of checking, reportedly looting gold and money. The Morung Express reports that he described the town as already full of army personnel before the shooting began. Imchen told the paper the operation appeared to have been premeditated. Army authorities are not reported in the pages consulted as having answered that claim.

The shooting started between roughly 10:00 and 10:30 a.m. A 1995 open letter from townspeople, addressed to the UN Secretary-General and later retrieved by the Morung Express, put the first shots at about 10:20 near the main shopping area, and said they struck several people including Lt Col K B Poonacha of the 16th Maratha Light Infantry. The letter said the army then began "a sudden, senseless and brutal yet systematic" assault on civilians, led by a Major Deepak Sharma of the 16th battalion. That is the townspeople's allegation, not a finding.

The army's version appears in a comment under Poonacha's page on Honourpoint, a memorial site for Indian soldiers. Brig Satish Malik wrote that at about 10:40 a.m. men from two rival factions of the National Socialist Council of Nagaland were trying to gain the upper hand over each other when the battalion's routine patrol arrived, that firing broke out from three sides and that the leading scout, Sep Rajaram Khot, was the first casualty. Poonacha, he wrote, came from a nearby base, was wounded in the hand and kept leading until another bullet killed him. In Malik's account eight insurgents died, all of one faction. A statement issued by Naga student and rights groups in Delhi in January 1995 also names an exchange of fire involving the NSCN, but says the colonel and seven others died and that the 16th battalion then took this as an excuse for revenge.

A survivor identified only as Medem told a Morung Express intern that he was in a fabric shop near the town square when firing began. He said the army told shopkeepers not to close up if they wanted to live, and that people caught outside were herded into the square and made to lie face down regardless of age or condition. He said the firing went on until about 4 p.m.

Imchen and the Delhi student statement described soldiers sealing the town from outside contact and posting men at key points, then using mortar shells and grenades on residential areas, in what the statement called a total contravention of the Geneva Conventions. People were forced to crawl along the streets and were herded together, the statement said. Imchen said threads, wool and cloth from the shops were soaked in kerosene and used to light the buildings, and that shutters were pulled down on people inside. Another Morung Express writer told of a man who was shot at by soldiers and survived, and who has kept the 18 bullet marks on his house. Because those writers are not neutral observers, all of this should be read as testimony.

One story from the same piece shows how long the aftermath lasted. A government servant, Yangchid, had hidden on the roof of a shop. His wife believed for weeks that he had escaped. His half-charred body was found only about a month later, when the burned building was pulled down.
content.h2: Counting the dead and the damage
content.p: The sources do not agree, and none of them is an official tally.
The Morung Express reported 11 civilians dead, 7 shot and 4 burned alive, plus several women raped.
The 1995 open letter gave 7 gunned down, 4 burned alive, and 89 shops, 48 houses, 17 vehicles and two two-wheelers destroyed.

Imchen, as quoted by the Morung Express, said seven civilians were shot, five more people, among them a child, were burned alive, and eight women were reportedly raped, with 89 shops, 49 houses, 17 vehicles and seven two-wheelers burned.
A 2024 Nagaland Tribune report, citing records and testimonies, listed five burned alive, two civilians shot and eight women sexually assaulted, with 84 houses, 89 shops and 24 vehicles destroyed.

The Mokokchung Times, citing the Delhi student statement, listed five burned to death, two civilians shot, three NSCN-K cadres and two army personnel including a colonel killed, and 84 houses, 89 shops, 17 vehicles and seven two-wheelers destroyed.

Some of these figures count only the civilians; others fold in the militants and soldiers who died in the first exchange of fire. Brig Malik's tribute lists eight insurgents killed instead of three. A 2020 statement by a local citizens' forum used the figures of 7 shot, 5 burned alive including a child, and dozens of women raped. A separate writer cited one citizens' investigation that reported 49 houses, 89 shops, seven shot, five burned alive and eight raped.

According to the Delhi student and rights groups, army headquarters issued a version that ignored the allegations of rape, looting and extortion and blamed the fires on a chain of exploding LPG cylinders, and the news agencies PTI and UNI carried this from Kohima. The statement also said the state government set up a three-member inquiry made up of officials from the Home Department, the police and the Assam Rifles, one of the forces accused. That is the groups' account; the pages consulted do not reproduce the army statement or the committee's report.

The townspeople went to the national rights body. M B Longkumer, convener of the Ao Senden Special Committee, was chosen as a one-man committee and travelled to Delhi on 17 January 1995. With help from the Naga Students' Union Delhi, the Naga People's Movement for Human Rights and a former member of parliament, he met the Commission's chairperson on 25 January. He recalled that its members were heartbroken when he showed them photographs and newspaper clippings. A public rally in Delhi on 28 January drew about 35 organisations, according to his account.

The Commission sent an investigating officer to Mokokchung on 5 February 1995, and on 26 April its chairperson and six members visited the town to meet victims and see the damage. Longkumer said the Commission promised to recommend an ex gratia payment of Rs 1 crore for the loss of life and property; a Morung Express writer likewise said the community obtained a compensation of Rs 1 crore. The Commission's own published summaries of its armed-forces cases, which are held by the University of Minnesota Human Rights Library, include an Assam Rifles case from Ukhrul in Manipur in the same 1994 to 1995 period, but the page consulted does not describe a Mokokchung finding, so the Commission's reasoning and the amount actually paid remain unsettled here. Imchen said that it was the testimony of eight women who came forward that brought the commission to Mokokchung.

Medem said many people who could afford it left. Those who could not stayed and rebuilt, and he went on to own his own shop. A Morung Express writer credited the community with managing much of the recovery itself, from clearing rubble to supporting businesses and building a memorial.

That memorial became a source of fresh anger. A monolith bearing the name Ayatai stood in the town, and a Morung Express report on a candlelight service by the Ao Students Conference said the existing Ayatai monolith would soon be replaced by a new one. In 2020 the Assam Rifles planned to open a war memorial in Mokokchung for personnel killed in insurgency. A statement from the Ao Concerned Citizen Forum, run in the Morung Express, called it an insult and wrote that the Indian Army had burned down the heart of Mokokchung town on 27 December 1994. By December 2024 the Ayatai monument had gone. Imchen asked why the Assam Rifles had a monolith listing personnel killed since 1951 while victims of Ayatai had none, and called its disappearance a sign that the Nagas' story had been ignored.

On 27 December 2024 townspeople held a candlelight service at the Main Police Point, led by Aowati Ozükum, vice president of the Ao Senden, with prayers by local Baptist pastors and a performance of a song titled Ayatai. A witness named Chuchang, a dobashi, told the Mokokchung Times that for him the police point was a graveyard. Imchen is described as convener of the Victims' Union 1994.

The reports from that day agree on one point, that accountability has not arrived. Longkumer said that no case had been registered in the Supreme Court. The Nagaland Tribune wrote that many questions remain unanswered, and the Mokokchung Times closed by saying the justice the townspeople seek has yet to come. None of the pages consulted reports a prosecution, a court-martial or a published inquiry finding against any soldier.
